facts.statement: Ilbandornis was an extinct genus of birds about the size of an ostrich.
facts.quote: Ilbandornis is an extinct genus of ostrich-sized dromornithid

facts.statement: Ilbandornis had a lighter build than other dromornithids, suggesting it was a fast runner.
facts.quote: It was far more lightly built than other members of the family, indicating a more cursorial lifestyle; it was a fast runner.

facts.statement: Most researchers believe Ilbandornis was herbivorous, supported by molecular analysis of its gastroliths and eggshells.
facts.quote: The majority of researchers consider Dromornithids to be herbivorous; this is borne out by molecular analysis of the gastroliths and eggshells of both Ilbandornis and the related Genyornis.

facts.statement: The dromornithid family is casually called "demon ducks" because they are closely related to waterfowl.
facts.quote: dromornithid, a clade known casually as "demon ducks" because they are most closely related to the water fowl clade anseriformes.

facts.statement: Ilbandornis were very large birds, with estimated masses ranging from that of an ostrich to twice that weight.
facts.quote: Ilbandornis were very large birds, with mass estimates spanning from similar to an Ostrich to twice that weight.

facts.statement: The species Ilbandornis woodburnei had estimated masses between 114 kg and 279 kg.
facts.quote: I. woodburnei estimates range from 114 kg to 279 kg

facts.statement: The species Ilbandornis lawsoni had estimated masses between 106 kg and 134 kg.
facts.quote: and I. lawsoni estimates at 106 to 134 kg.

facts.statement: Patricia Vickers-Rich named two species of Ilbandornis in 1979.
facts.quote: Two species named by Patricia Vickers-Rich in 1979 were included in the genus

facts.statement: Fossils of Ilbandornis species were found in the Waite Formation at the Alcoota Fossil Beds in Australia's Northern Territory.
facts.quote: both of which are known from the Alcoota Fossil Beds in the Northern Territory, from Waite Formation sediments dating to the Late Miocene.

facts.statement: Ilbandornis went extinct during the Miocene epoch.
facts.quote: Ilbandornis went extinct sometime in the Miocene epoch.

facts.statement: The fossils of Ilbandornis date to the Late Miocene.
Some researchers debate whether Ilbandornis lawsoni should remain in its own genus or be classified as a species of Genyornis or synonymous with I. woodburnei.
facts.quote: some researchers argue that the inclusion of both species within the genus is problematic, since I. lawsoni is either considered a species of Genyornis or synonymous with I. woodburnei.

facts.statement: Ilbandornis belongs to the family Dromornithidae.
The genus Ilbandornis was established by P. Rich in 1979.
The fossil record for Ilbandornis spans from the Tortonian to the Late Pleistocene, between 11.63 and 0.0117 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Tortonian to Late Pleistocene (11.63 to 0.0117 million years ago)
